content.intro: Learn entity-relationship modeling through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Entity-Relationship Modeling matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use entity-relationship modeling to connect business meaning to table structure. A reliable relational design states what one row represents, how records are identified, and how related facts are connected without accidental duplication.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Entities and attributes, Primary and foreign keys in diagrams, Cardinality and optionality, Mapping relationships into tables. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Entities and attributes
items.text: Entities and attributes is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Primary and foreign keys in diagrams
items.text: Primary and foreign keys in diagrams should be expressed as a database rule where practical, not only as an application convention. Test duplicate values and missing references so that invalid states are rejected consistently.

items.title: Cardinality and optionality
items.text: Cardinality and optionality is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Mapping relationships into tables
items.text: Mapping relationships into tables helps you learn how rows, columns, keys, relationships, schemas, and normalization work together to represent real-world facts without avoidable duplication. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Designing a database from requirements
items.text: Designing a database from requirements helps you learn how rows, columns, keys, relationships, schemas, and normalization work together to represent real-world facts without avoidable duplication. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT o.order_id, c.full_name, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC;
content_blocks.expected_output: Each order is paired with its customer through the foreign-key relationship. The unique tie-breaker makes the requested order deterministic.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
